cards.title: 3.1 What is Ecology?
body: Ecology comes from the Greek words “oikos” (“house” or “place where one lives”) and “logos” (“study of”).
Ecology then means the study of the “house” in which organisms live.
An understanding of ecology is essential for the survival of humankind.

Understanding the structure and function of the various levels of ecological hierarchies and the relationships between them is vitally important for the well-being of humanity and for life in general.
Ecology is also a science that contributes considerably to the understanding of evolution.

cards.title: 3.1 What is ecology?
body: **Ecology** is the study of relationships among organisms and between organisms and their environment.

- **Species** — organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring.
- **Population** — members of one species in one area.
- **Community** — all populations interacting in an area.
- **Ecosystem** — community + abiotic environment.
- **Habitat** — the physical place a species lives.
- **Niche** — its role (what it eats, when, where, how it affects others).
- **Biosphere** — all ecosystems on Earth.
- **Biome** — a group of ecosystems with similar climate and dominant communities.

**Abiotic factors:** water, soil, pH, salinity, N and P, temperature, light, natural disasters. **Biotic factors:** all living influences (predation, competition, disease, human action such as deforestation).
Population growth depends on birth rate and death rate; most populations can grow exponentially while resources last.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: The scientific term used to describe the place where an organism actually lives within an ecosystem is its:

steps.text: - **Habitat:** The physical location or address where an organism lives (e.g., forest floor).
- **Niche:** The functional role or job of an organism in its ecosystem.
**Result:** The physical place is called the **Habitat**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A dry, treeless polar biome characterized by the presence of a permanently frozen layer of subsoil called permafrost is the:
cards.why:
**Given:** Biome characteristics.

**Formula/Rule:** The **Tundra** is a polar biome defined by cold temperatures, low rainfall, lack of trees, and a permanently frozen layer of subsoil called **permafrost**.

**Result:** The biome described is the **Tundra**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following environmental factors is classified as a biotic factor?
cards.why:
**Given:** Ecological factors.

**Formula/Rule:** 
- **Abiotic factors** are non-living physical and chemical elements (temperature, soil pH, salinity, water).
- **Biotic factors** are living biological interactions (parasitism, predation, mutualism).

**Result:** **Parasitism** is a biotic factor.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The scientific term used to describe the place where an organism actually lives within an ecosystem is its:
cards.why:
**Given:** Definitions of ecological spatial terms.

**Formula/Rule:** 
- **Habitat:** The physical location or address where an organism lives (e.g., forest floor).
- **Niche:** The functional role or job of an organism in its ecosystem.

**Result:** The physical place is called the **Habitat**.

cards.title: 3.2 Natural cycles
body: Atoms are reused. Learn the path and the key processes, not every arrow.

cards.title: Carbon cycle
body: CO₂ in air → photosynthesis into organic carbon → food chains → respiration returns CO₂. Combustion of fossil fuels and wood adds extra CO₂. Decomposition and the ocean are major stores/exchanges.

cards.title: Oxygen cycle
body: Photosynthesis releases O₂; respiration and combustion consume it. Tightly linked to the carbon cycle.

cards.title: Nitrogen cycle
body: Air is ~78% N₂, unusable by most organisms. **Nitrogen fixation** (bacteria, some cyanobacteria; also lightning) makes ammonia. Nitrifying bacteria make nitrites then nitrates that plants absorb. Animals eat plants. Denitrifying bacteria return N₂ to air. Decomposition / ammonification recycle organic N.

cards.title: Water cycle
body: Evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, runoff, infiltration. Driven by the sun.

cards.title: 3.2 Natural cycles
body: **Phosphorus cycle** has no major atmospheric gas stage. Phosphate weathers from rock into soil and water, is taken up by producers, moves through food chains, and returns via decomposition and sedimentation. Often a limiting nutrient; excess from fertiliser causes water pollution.

cards.title: Carbon–oxygen handshake: in photosynthesis plants take in CO₂ and give out O₂; respiration (in animals, and in plants too, especially at night) does the reverse.
Mnemonic — Fix Nitrify Assimilate Denitrify
body: Nitrogen: bacteria *fix* N₂ → ammonia; others *nitrify* to nitrite then nitrate; plants *assimilate* nitrate; other bacteria *denitrify* back to N₂.
Phosphorus is the “rock cycle nutrient” — almost no air stage. If a question says “no gaseous phase”, pick phosphorus.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What primary producers float on the surface of the marine biome, carrying out photosynthesis?
cards.why:
**Given:** Ocean primary producers.

**Formula/Rule:** Microscopic, single-celled photosynthetic organisms that drift in the sunlit upper layer of oceans are called **phytoplankton** (e.g., diatoms), acting as the ultimate producers of the marine biome.

**Result:** The primary producers are **Phytoplankton**.

steps.text: **Formula/Rule:** Microscopic, single-celled photosynthetic organisms that drift in the sunlit upper layer of oceans are called **phytoplankton** (e.g., diatoms), acting as the ultimate producers of the marine biome.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following is not involved in water cycle
cards.why:
**Transcription** is a biological process in genetics where DNA is copied into RNA. It has nothing to do with the water cycle. 

- **Transpiration:** Water loss from plants.
- **Evaporation:** Water turning to vapor.
- **Precipitation:** Rain/Snow.
- **Condensation:** Vapor turning to liquid.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following nutrient cycles is unique because it lacks a gaseous atmospheric phase and depends entirely on rock weathering?
cards.why:
**Given:** Features of nutrient cycles.

**Formula/Rule:** The **Phosphorus cycle** does not involve the atmosphere and has no gaseous phase. Phosphorus is locked in rock formations and is released slowly into soil through weathering.

**Result:** The cycle is the **Phosphorus cycle**.

steps.text: **Formula/Rule:** The **Phosphorus cycle** does not involve the atmosphere and has no gaseous phase. Phosphorus is locked in rock formations and is released slowly into soil through weathering.

cards.title: 3.3 Food relationships
body: **Producers** (autotrophs, mainly photosynthesising plants and algae) convert inorganic carbon to food. **Consumers** (heterotrophs): primary (herbivores), secondary, tertiary. **Decomposers** (bacteria, fungi) recycle nutrients.
A **food chain** is one linear feeding path, e.g.
grass → grasshopper → lizard → hawk
A **food web** is the interlinked set of chains in a community — more realistic, more stable.

cards.title: 3.3 Food relationships
head: Relationship
Who benefits?
Example
rows: Parasite lives on or in a host and harms it (tapeworm, ticks, some fungi).
One benefits, the other is unaffected (e.g. epiphytes on trees).
Both benefit (N-fixing bacteria in roots; lichens; cleaner fish).
Predator kills and eats prey; important population control.

cards.title: Food chain and the direction of energy flow
body: The arrow in a food chain always shows the direction of energy flow. Each organism uses some energy, so there is less for the next level; most food chains have fewer than five links. Decomposers are placed at the end.

cards.title: 3.3.1 Food Chains
body: As energy is transferred along the chain, each organism uses some of it.
Producers have more energy available to them than consumers, thus, they are usually numerous in number.
The loss of energy along the food chain also limits its length.
For example a green plant is eaten by a herbivore and the herbivore is eaten by a carnivore.

cards.title: 3.3.2 Food Webs
body: In a community where organisms live and interact, simple food chains rarely exist, because most often the same food resource is part of more than one chain.
A food web is composed of several interconnecting food chains.
Grass is eaten by grasshoppers, which are in turn eaten by a chicken.
In the second example grass is eaten by a sheep and the sheep could then be consumed by a leopard or hyena.

cards.title: 3.3.3 Parasitism
body: **Parasitism** is a symbiotic relationship in which an organism obtains nutrients from another living organism without killing it.
A parasite benefits in terms of food and shelter, whereas the host is harmed in some way.

Parasites found inside the body of the host are known as **endo-parasites e**.g. tapeworm, Plasmodium sp., etc., whereas those parasites found on the surface of a host are called ectoparasites e.g. tick.
Natural selection favours parasites that are best able to locate and feed on the host.

cards.title: 3.3.4 Commensalism
body: Few absolute examples exist since it is unusual for one organism not to be affected in some way by a close association with another organism.
Commensalism is, however, observed in tree-roosting birds.
The trees gain nothing in return, but are not harmed by the interaction.
The remoras swim alongside the shark as it moves through the water.

cards.title: 3.3.5 Mutualism
body: A change in either organism is likely to affect the survival and reproduction of the other.
Mutualistic relationships occurs among symbiotic bacteria, such as Rhizobium bacteria in the root nodules of leguminous plants (e.g. beans or peas).
Rhizobium spp. are bacteria capable of fixing atmospheric nitrogen, which is changed into nitrates.
Plants absorb nitrates from the soil and use them for producing food, like proteins, carbohydrates and lipids.

cards.title: 3.3.6 Predation
body: The prey constitutes an organism that is hunted and killed by the predator.
Predation can occur between a hyena and a goat.
Nevertheless, some herbivores, like bark beetles, eat plant parts and often harm the plant without killing it.
Predators have a number of adaptive characteristics which make them efficient in capturing their prey.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which biological processes drive the rapid cycling of carbon between the atmosphere and organic life?
cards.why:
**Given:** Carbon cycle processes.

**Formula/Rule:** 
- **Photosynthesis** absorbs atmospheric $$\text{CO}_2$$ to make organic molecules.
- **Cellular Respiration** breaks down these organic molecules to release $$\text{CO}_2$$ back into the atmosphere.

**Result:** The correct processes are **Photosynthesis and Cellular Respiration**.

cards.problem: Which biological processes drive the rapid cycling of carbon between the atmosphere and organic life?

steps.text:
**Formula/Rule:** 
- **Photosynthesis** absorbs atmospheric $$\text{CO}_2$$ to make organic molecules.
- **Cellular Respiration** breaks down these organic molecules to release $$\text{CO}_2$$ back into the atmosphere.
**Result:** The correct processes are **Photosynthesis and Cellular Respiration**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: During the nitrogen cycle, which group of bacteria is responsible for converting toxic nitrites ($$\text{NO}_2^-$$) into non-toxic nitrates ($$\text{NO}_3^-$$)?
cards.why:
**Given:** Nitrifying bacteria.

**Formula/Rule:** 
- *Nitrosomonas* converts ammonium ($$\text{NH}_4^+$$) into nitrites ($$\text{NO}_2^-$$).
- *Nitrobacter* converts nitrites ($$\text{NO}_2^-$$) into nitrates ($$\text{NO}_3^-$$).

**Result:** The bacteria responsible are **Nitrobacter**.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: During the nitrogen cycle, which group of bacteria is responsible for converting toxic nitrites ($$\text{NO}_2^-$$) into non-toxic nitrates ($$\text{NO}_3^-$$)?

steps.text:
**Formula/Rule:** 
- *Nitrosomonas* converts ammonium ($$\text{NH}_4^+$$) into nitrites ($$\text{NO}_2^-$$).
- *Nitrobacter* converts nitrites ($$\text{NO}_2^-$$) into nitrates ($$\text{NO}_3^-$$).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: ___________is a **symbiotic** relationship in which an organism obtains nutrients from another living organism **without killing it**.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define the relationships.** 
- **Predation:** One kills and eats another.
- **Mutualism:** Both benefit.
- **Commensalism:** One benefits, other is unaffected.
- **Parasitism:** One (parasite) benefits by taking nutrients from another (host), usually harming but not immediately killing it.
**Step 2: Conclusion.** The description matches **parasitism**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A type of symbiotic association in which one organism benefits & the other one is harmed
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Define the relationships.
- Commensalism: (+/0) One benefits, other unaffected.
- **Parasitism:** (+/-) One benefits (parasite), other harmed (host).
- Mutualism: (+/+) Both benefit.
- **Predation:** (+/-) One benefits (predator), other harmed/killed (prey).
**Step 2:** Since both Parasitism and Predation involve one organism benefiting at the expense of another being harmed, the answer is E.

cards.title: 3.4 Ecological pyramids
body:
- **Pyramid of numbers** — count of organisms at each trophic level. Usually upright; can invert (one tree feeding many insects).
- **Pyramid of biomass** — dry mass at each level. Usually upright on land; can invert in some oceans (phytoplankton reproduce so fast that a small standing crop supports more zooplankton).
- **Pyramid of energy** — energy flow per unit time. *Always* upright because energy is lost as heat at each transfer (~10% rule is the useful exam figure).

cards.title: Pyramid of energy
body: Producers form the large base. Energy is lost at each transfer, so each higher trophic level has less. That is why the pyramid of energy is always upright, while pyramids of numbers and biomass can be inverted.

cards.title: Energy pyramid — always a triangle pointing up. Only ~10% of energy climbs each step.
Mnemonic — +/− relationships
body: Parasite = unwelcome housemate (− host). Commensal = hitchhiker (0 host). Mutual = teammates (+ +). Predator = hunter (+ / − but prey dies).
Numbers and biomass pyramids can stand on their heads. Energy never does — heat leaks out.

cards.title: 3.4.1 Pyramids of Numbers
body: The same is done for the next step of primary producers, and so on.
When pyramids of numbers are drawn to scale, the food relationships produce a pyramid-shaped histogram called the pyramid of numbers.
The size of each block in the pyramid represents the numbers of organisms feeding at that level.
The pyramid-shaped histogram indicates a decrease in the amount of energy and number of organisms as it goes up through the trophic levels.

cards.title: 3.4.2 Pyramids of Biomass
body: The biomass of an organism is its constant total dry weight in the ecosystem.
Biomass is expressed in terms of grams per square metre (g/m2) or in metric tons (t) per hectare (ha) of material.
The shape of the pyramid narrows sharply from producers at the base to carnivores at the apex.
The producers have, then, the highest biomass per unit of area and, in decreasing order, are followed by primary-, secondary-, tertiaryand quaternary consumers.

cards.title: 3.4.3 Pyramids of Energy
body: The size of the boxes (blocks) represents the quantity of energy in the organisms.
Pyramids of energy are based on the amount of energy produced per unit area (often per square centimetre) by different tropic levels over a given period of time (typically per annum).
Pyramids of energy give a more accurate picture of the decreasing amounts of energy flowing through successive trophic levels of an ecosystem.
The rate of production of primary producers is termed “primary productivity”.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The destructive environmental phenomenon of acid rain is chemically initiated by the release of which air pollutants?
cards.why:
**Given:** Acid rain causes.

**Formula/Rule:** Acid rain is formed when **sulfur dioxide ($$\text{SO}_2$$)** and **nitrogen oxides ($$\text{NO}_x$$)**, produced by industrial combustion, react with atmospheric water vapor to synthesize sulfuric and nitric acids.

**Result:** The initiating pollutants are **Sulfur dioxide and Nitrogen oxides**.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: The destructive environmental phenomenon of acid rain is chemically initiated by the release of which air pollutants?

steps.text: **Formula/Rule:** Acid rain is formed when **sulfur dioxide ($$\text{SO}_2$$)** and **nitrogen oxides ($$\text{NO}_x$$)**, produced by industrial combustion, react with atmospheric water vapor to synthesize sulfuric and nitric acids.
**Result:** The initiating pollutants are **Sulfur dioxide and Nitrogen oxides**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In the natural ecosystem, the number of individuals often ________ as one moves from producers to top consumers.
cards.why: In most ecosystems, there are many more producers (plants) than primary consumers (herbivores), and many more herbivores than top predators (carnivores). This is because energy is lost at each level, supporting fewer individuals at the top.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following describes the correct order of ecological organization from the simplest level to the most complex?
cards.why:
**Given:** Levels of ecological organization.

**Formula/Rule:** The correct hierarchy from smallest (least complex) to largest (most complex) is:
$$\text{Organism} \rightarrow \text{Population} \rightarrow \text{Community} \rightarrow \text{Ecosystem} \rightarrow \text{Biome} \rightarrow \text{Biosphere}$$

**Result:** The correct sequence is **Organism, Population, Community, Ecosystem, Biome**.

cards.title: 3.5 Biomes of the World
body: **An ecosystem** is a complete, life-supporting environment.
Ecosystems can be grouped according to their similarities into major ecosystems called biomes.
The major biomes of the world are classified as terrestrial and aquatic biomes.
The terrestrial biomes vary according to the type of vegetation, the climate or the dominant organisms that inhabit them.
Tropical rain forest: Tropical rain forests are located in the equatorial belt.

cards.title: 3.5 Biomes of the world
body: A biome is recognised mainly by climate and dominant vegetation.

cards.title: 3.5 Biomes of the world
head: Biome
Climate & look
Exam notes for Eritrea / Africa
rows: Highest rainfall, high year-round temperature, huge biodiversity, layered trees
Present in Africa; not a major Eritrean biome
Seasonal rain, grasses + scattered trees, large herbivores
Savanna is a grassland biome; found in Africa and Eritrea
Very low rain; hot days, cold nights; sparse drought-adapted life
Four seasons, trees that drop leaves
Long cold winters, conifers, soil may be acidic
Permanently frozen soil (permafrost), low plants, brief summer

cards.title: 3.5 Biomes of the world
body: Marine systems in the syllabus include the Red Sea (coral reefs). Open-ocean producers are mainly single-celled phytoplankton.

cards.title: Exam map for Eritrea
body: Present: desert, grassland/savanna. Not present: taiga, tundra. Tropical rainforest exists in Africa but is not a major Eritrean biome in the review items.
**Hottest days + coldest nights = desert.** Highest rain = tropical rainforest. Permafrost = tundra. Conifers + long winter = taiga.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A symbiotic association where one organism benefits while the other is completely unaffected (neither helped nor harmed) is called:
cards.why:
**Given:** Symbiosis definitions.

**Formula/Rule:** 
- **Mutualism:** Both benefit ($$+/+$$).
- **Parasitism:** One benefits, one is harmed ($$+/-$$).
- **Commensalism:** One benefits, one is unaffected ($$+/0$$).

**Result:** The relationship is **Commensalism**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which type of ecological pyramid compares the rate of energy flow through each trophic level and can never be inverted?
cards.why:
**Given:** Trophic structure pyramids.

**Formula/Rule:** The **Pyramid of Energy** shows rate of energy flow. Due to the Second Law of Thermodynamics, energy is lost at each transfer. Therefore, it is **never inverted** and is always upright.

**Result:** The pyramid is the **Pyramid of Energy**.

cards.problem: Which type of ecological pyramid compares the rate of energy flow through each trophic level and can never be inverted?

steps.text: **Formula/Rule:** The **Pyramid of Energy** shows rate of energy flow. Due to the Second Law of Thermodynamics, energy is lost at each transfer. Therefore, it is **never inverted** and is always upright.
**Result:** The pyramid is the **Pyramid of Energy**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which biome has very low rainfall, extreme temperatures and plants such as cacti with thick stems and spines?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Deserts receive less than about 250 mm of rain a year.

**Step 2:** Plants are adapted to store water and reduce water loss (spines, thick cuticles).

**Step 3:** Rainforests are wet; tundra is cold; deciduous forests have moderate rain.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

cards.title: 3.6 Natural resources and survival
body: **Renewable resources** can be replaced on a human timescale if used carefully: air, water, forests, solar energy, living wildlife. **Non-renewable resources** exist in finite stocks formed over geological time: coal, oil, natural gas, most minerals.

**Pollution** is the release of harmful wastes into the environment — air (SO₂ → acid rain; smoke), water (sewage, fertiliser, oil), soil, noise, and damage to the **ozone layer** that screens UV radiation. Acid rain corrodes metals, damages buildings and can kill fish; ozone thinning is a separate problem (UV), not caused by acid rain.
**Conservation** is protection and wise use: reforestation (opposite of deforestation), wildlife reserves, sustainable harvesting, reducing emissions, protecting the ozone layer.

cards.title: Key takeaways
body: ★ DNA stores, RNA delivers, protein does the work. ★ Mitosis copies; meiosis shuffles and halves. ★ 3:1 and 9:3:3:1 are the exam ratios. ★ Dad’s Y decides sex; X-linked hits sons harder.

cards.title: Quick formulas / ratios
body: A–T, G–C · codon = 3 bases F₂ mono 3:1 · dihybrid 9:3:3:1 Test cross 1:1 (or 1:1:1:1) ~10% energy per trophic step

cards.title: Remember for exams
body: ✓ Learn exact definitions (gene, allele, genotype, phenotype, species). ✓ Draw Punnett squares — don’t guess. ✓ Separate Lamarck from Darwin. ✓ Energy pyramid cannot invert.

cards.title: 3.6.1 Types of Natural Resources
body: Renewable resources are those resources that are mainly living things, together with their products.
Non-renewable resources are those that are non-living e.g. rocks, minerals and the products of things that were once alive, like coal and petroleum.
Humans are constantly modifying their biological environment to satisfy their needs.
Other serious problems concerning humankind’s impact on the environment include pollution, deforestation and erosion.

cards.title: 3.6.2 Pollution
body: Any agent which causes pollution is called a **pollutant**.
The types of pollutant and their effects have greatly increased in modern times because of urbanization, overpopulation and the development of industries.
Air pollution: The harmful effects of many air pollutants are considerable.
The poisonous gases that pollute the air are sulphur dioxide, oxides of nitrogen, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, lead smoke, radiation and chloroflurocarbons (CFCs).

cards.title: 3.6.3 Conservation
body: If people are to continue to exist in the future, certain measures must be taken to ensure that adequate resources are available and pollution is controlled.
The objectives of conservation are to preserve existing natural resources, restore renewable resources and practice wise management of all non-renewable resources.

Although a number of conservation programs are in effect at present, such as the summer reforestation program and community-based building of terraces, much more needs to be done to conserve and protect Eritrea’s resources of soil, water, wildlife, atmosphere and minerals.
When people became aware of the fact that rich, productive soil had become scarce, conservation became a necessity.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In a food chain, green plants (producers) are classified as occupying which of the following trophic levels?
cards.why:
**Given:** Trophic level organization.

**Formula/Rule:** In all food chains, the primary producers (autotrophs) are positioned at the bottom, occupying **Trophic Level 1**. Primary consumers occupy Trophic Level 2.

**Result:** Green plants occupy **Trophic Level 1**.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: In a food chain, green plants (producers) are classified as occupying which of the following trophic levels?

steps.text: **Formula/Rule:** In all food chains, the primary producers (autotrophs) are positioned at the bottom, occupying **Trophic Level 1**. Primary consumers occupy Trophic Level 2.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: On average, what percentage of energy from one trophic level is successfully incorporated into the organic tissues of the next trophic level?
cards.why:
**Given:** Ecological transfer efficiency.

**Formula/Rule:** Lindeman's Ten Percent Law states that only about **$$10\%$$** of net energy at one trophic level is transferred and incorporated into the next level, while $$90\%$$ is lost as heat.

**Result:** The percentage is **$$10\%$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following is a renewable exhaustible natural resource?
cards.why: Renewable resources can be replenished. However, 'exhaustible' implies that if used faster than they are replaced, they can run out. **Biomass** (wood, crops, animal waste) is renewable because we can grow more plants, but it is exhaustible if we cut forests faster than they grow back.

Biotic factors are the factors that affect a given ecosystem, and include all living elements.

Trophic level refers to the feeding relationship.
Denitrification is the opposite of nitrogen fixation and converts nitrates (NO3) and nitrites (NO2) in the soil into nitrogen gas or gaseous compounds, such as nitrous oxide or nitric oxide.

Nitrification is a vital part of the nitrogen cycle, wherein certain soil bacteria are able to transform the ammonium that is produced by the decomposition of proteins into nitrates, making them available to plants.

tips.text: Ecology is the study of the relationships between different living organisms, and the interactions between organisms and their physical environment.
Ecology endeavours to understand the various levels of ecological hierarchies and their functions.
The place where living organisms dwell is called a habitat.
The way of life, which enables a species to occupy a particular place within a community, is a niche.
A group of individuals of the same species living in the same geographic area is called a population.
Collectively, all the living things in a given area that interact with one another are referred to as a community.
Communities have different sizes and boundaries.
The sum total of living organisms interacting with one another and their non-living environment in a given area is termed an ecosystem.
Ecosystems can be roughly divided into terrestrial-, freshwaterand marine ecosystems.
A group of ecosystems, characterized by their climate, soil and geographic location, make up a biome.

Key takeaways: ★ DNA stores, RNA delivers, protein does the work. ★ Mitosis copies; meiosis shuffles and halves. ★ 3:1 and 9:3:3:1 are the exam ratios. ★ Dad’s Y decides sex; X-linked hits sons harder.
Quick formulas / ratios: A–T, G–C · codon = 3 bases F₂ mono 3:1 · dihybrid 9:3:3:1 Test cross 1:1 (or 1:1:1:1) ~10% energy per trophic step
Remember for exams: ✓ Learn exact definitions (gene, allele, genotype, phenotype, species). ✓ Draw Punnett squares — don’t guess. ✓ Separate Lamarck from Darwin. ✓ Energy pyramid cannot invert.

items.text: In ecology, the ____, or natural cycle, is a pathway by which inorganic substances move through both biotic and abiotic elements of the ecosystem.
Among the major terrestrial ____ are the tropical rain forest, temperate deciduous forest, taiga, tundra, grassland, desert and life zones in mountains.
____ are the factors that affect a given ecosystem, and include all living elements.
____ is a symbiotic relationship in which an organism obtains nutrients from another living organism without killing it.
Another example of ____ is the relationship between a shark and the small remora fish.
Parasites found inside the body of the ____ are known as endo-parasites e.g. tapeworm, Plasmodium sp., etc., whereas those parasites found on the surface of a host are called ectoparasites e.g. tick.
____ is a relationship in which both symbiotic organisms benefit from each other.
____ is a food relationship in which an organism (predator) kills another (prey) for food.

questions.q: Photosynthesis and respiration belong to the ________ cycle.
why: Photosynthesis removes CO₂ from the air and releases O₂; respiration releases CO₂ and uses O₂ — together they cycle carbon (and oxygen) between organisms and the atmosphere.
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: The Carbon Cycle involves  A) respiration.  B) photosynthesis.  C) decomposition.  D) industry by-products.  E) All of the above.
similar.a: E. All of the above. — Carbon moves from the air into organisms by photosynthesis and returns to the air by respiration, decomposition of dead organisms and combustion of fuels (including industrial emissions). Answer: E.

questions.q: Nitrogen cycle is carried out primarily by ________.
why: Bacteria do every key step of the nitrogen cycle: nitrogen fixation (Rhizobium, Azotobacter), nitrification (Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter), denitrification, and decomposition to ammonium.
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: Animals depend on bacteria and fungi because bacteria and fungi  A) do not perform photosynthesis.  B) recycle nutrients in dead organisms.  C) use sunlight to produce sugar.  D) provide animal habitat.  E) are parasites.
similar.a: B. recycle nutrients in dead organisms. — Bacteria and fungi are decomposers: they break down dead organisms and wastes, returning nutrients (N, P, C) to the soil and air for producers, on which animals ultimately depend. Answer: B.

questions.q: Physical place a species lives: ________.
why: A habitat is the physical place where an organism lives, e.g. a pond or the bark of a tree; its niche is its role there.
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: In which terrestrial biome do you usually observe high diversity of species?  A) Tundra  B) Taiga  C) Equatorial rain forest  D) Grasslands  E) None
similar.a: C. Equatorial rain forest — Tundra and taiga are cold with few species; grasslands have moderate diversity. Answer: C.

questions.q: Non-living factors: ________.
why: Abiotic factors are the non-living parts of the environment: temperature, light, water, soil, wind, pH. Biotic factors are the living organisms.
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

questions.q: Conifer-forest biome: ________.
why: The taiga (boreal forest) is a cold northern biome dominated by evergreen conifers such as pine, spruce and fir.
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: A terrestrial biome that is characterized by low rainfall and the presence of shrubs and small trees is  A) temperate deciduous forest.  B) taiga.  C) life zones in mountains.  D) desert.  E) grass land.
similar.a: E. grass land. — Deserts have VERY low and infrequent rainfall; taiga is a cold coniferous forest; temperate deciduous forests have moderate-to-high rainfall. Answer: E.

questions.q: Highest-rainfall biome: ________.
why: Tropical rainforests near the equator receive the most rain (often over 2 000 mm a year) and are warm all year.
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: The lowest level of environmental complexity that includes living and nonliving things is the  A) biome.  B) species.  C) community.  D) ecosystem.  E) biosphere.
similar.a: D. ecosystem. — An ecosystem is a community plus its nonliving (abiotic) environment – the lowest level with both. Biome and biosphere are higher levels. Answer: D.

questions.q: Savanna is part of the ________ biome.
why: Savanna is a tropical grassland with scattered trees and a long dry season, so it belongs to the grassland biome.
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: The type of vegetation in a given biome is not greatly influenced by  A) the type of organisms that inhabit it.  B) temperature.  C) rainfall.  D) soil type.  E) None of the above.
similar.a: A. the type of organisms that inhabit it. — The animals living there depend on the vegetation rather than determining it. Answer: A.

questions.q: Biome not found in Africa: ________.
why: Taiga (and tundra) need long, very cold winters found only at high northern latitudes; Africa lies between about 37°N and 35°S, so it has no taiga.
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

questions.q: Not renewable: ________ (e.g. natural gas).
why: Natural gas, coal and oil (fossil fuels) form over millions of years, so once used they cannot be replaced on a human time scale — they are non-renewable.
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: Denitrification converts  A) nitrogen gas into nitrate and nitrite.  B) nitrogen into ammonium salt and ammonia.  C) nitrates and nitrites into nitrogen gas.  D) ammonium salts into nitrates.  E) ammonium salts into nitrous gas and nitrite.
similar.a: C. nitrates and nitrites into nitrogen gas. — B = nitrogen fixation; D = nitrification. Answer: C.

questions.q: Earth is shielded from UV by the ________.
why: The ozone (O₃) layer in the stratosphere absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation.
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: Which pyramid cannot be inverted?  A) Numbers  B) Energy  C) Biomass  D) None of them can invert

questions.q: Which pyramid cannot be inverted?
why: Answer B: Energy
Energy is lost at every trophic level (as heat), so each level always has less energy than the one below; a pyramid of numbers (one tree, many insects) or biomass can be inverted.
questions.tip: Read all the options before you choose; cross out the ones that belong to a different idea.

similar.q: The pyramid that can never be inverted in an ecological trophic level is the  A) pyramid of numbers.  B) pyramid of biomass.  C) pyramid of energy.  D) All can be inverted.  E) All can’t be inverted.
similar.a: C. pyramid of energy. — Pyramids of numbers (e.g. one tree with many insects) and of biomass (e.g. in water) can be inverted. Answer: C.

questions.q: Which biome is NOT found in Africa?
why: Answer C: Taiga
Taiga is a cold conifer forest of high northern latitudes. Africa has tropical rainforest, grassland (savanna) and desert.

why: **Species interaction** (like predation or competition) is a **biotic** factor because it involves living organisms. Abiotic factors are non-living components like temperature, water, and soil minerals.

questions.q: One of the following is **not found** in the ecological level of organization.
why:
**Step 1:** Define ecological levels. Ecology studies how living things interact with each other and their environment. The levels are: Organism → Population → Community → Ecosystem → Biosphere.
**Step 2:** Define biological/internal levels. These are levels *within* an individual: Cell → Tissue → Organ → **Organ system**.
**Step 3:** Differentiate. An **Organ system** is a group of organs working together inside a body. It is a level of biological organization, but not a level of *ecological* organization.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: The bacteria that responsible for oxidation of nitrites to nitrates is:
why: In the nitrogen cycle, **Nitrobacter** (spelled 'Nirobactera' in the options) is responsible for converting nitrites ($$ NO_2^- $$) into nitrates ($$ NO_3^- $$). This process is called nitrification.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Which Biome has succulent plants?
why: Succulent plants (like cacti) are adapted to store water in their thick, fleshy stems or leaves, which is a key survival strategy in the **Desert** biome where water is scarce.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Which one of the following bacteria is not involved in nitrogen cycle?
why:
All listed bacteria play a role in the nitrogen cycle:
- **Nitrosomonas (A):** Converts ammonia to nitrites (Nitrification).
- **Pseudomonas (B):** Converts nitrates back to nitrogen gas (Denitrification).
- **Nitrobacter (C):** Converts nitrites to nitrates (Nitrification).
- **Clostridium (D):** A free-living bacteria that fixes atmospheric nitrogen.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: All are non-living components of an ecosystem, **except**
why: Non-living (abiotic) factors include water, soil, air, and land. Planktons are living (biotic) microscopic organisms found in water ecosystems.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: A biome includes all of the following, **except**
why: A biome is a large geographical area defined by its climate, soil, and types of ecosystems. While humans live within biomes, they are **not a defining biological or physical component** of a biome's classification.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Which of the following species of **bacteria** is involved in the conversion of **ammonia or ammonium into nitrites**?
why:
**Step 1: Review the Nitrogen Cycle.** Nitrification is a two-step process.
**Step 2: Identify the bacteria for each step.** 
- Step 1: Ammonia ($$ NH_3 $$) $$\rightarrow$$ Nitrites ($$ NO_2^- $$) is performed by **Nitrosomonas**.
- Step 2: Nitrites ($$ NO_2^- $$) $$\rightarrow$$ Nitrates ($$ NO_3^- $$) is performed by **Nitrobacter**.
**Step 3: Conclusion.** The question asks for the conversion to nitrites, so Nitrosomonas is correct.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.
